description: Undergraduate data science student engineering the Lunar Site Navigator solo for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The project deterministically computes solar power and direct-to-Earth communication windows for lunar South Pole candidate landing sites by fusing NASA JPL Horizons API ephemeris scraping through the real-time data and building a complete web-based visualization tool keeping in mind the huge spectrum of users : comprising of learners, educators and mission planners, space researchers
summary: Lunar Selenix is web-based decision-making support tool that helps mission planners, educators, and students evaluate candidate lunar landing sites using real-time ephemeris data from NASA JPL'S Horizon API System. Users select any selenographic coordinate on a interactive 3D Moon globe an instantly receive a full-cycle analysis: solar illumination patterns, Earth visibility windows for DTE(direct-to-earth communication), irradiance curves and battery sizing/storage estimates. The tool features a dual mode interface - "Explorer Mode" with animated visualization for learners, explorers and educators whereas the "Planner Mode" with data-dense tables and relative data charts for the mission engineers and planners for a clear graphical view and data interpreted through graphical curves. A compare view ranks upto 10 candidate sites using customizable weighted scoring across criteria like sunlit percentage, longest blackout duration, and communication availability. Nine real artemis-era selected sites are build in as presets. All computation derive from actual JPL Horizons ephemeris system API - no approximations, no static datasets.
details:
What it does:
Lunar Selenix evaluates any point on the Moon’s surface as a potential landing or base site. Given a selenographic coordinate and a time window, it computes sun elevation and azimuth, earth elevation and visibility, solar irradiance on both flat and tilted panels, and battery requirements to survive darkness periods — all from real JPL Horizons ephemeris data queried in real time.

How it works:
The backend is a Python/Flask API that calls NASA’s JPL Horizons API to retrieve Sun and Earth positions as observed from a user-specified point on the lunar surface. It computes solar geometry, irradiance using the inverse-square law and cosine correction, classifies each timestep into illumination and communication states, and generates summary statistics. The frontend is a React application using Three.js (React Three Fiber) for an interactive 3D Moon globe with NASA lunar texture, Recharts for timeline charts, and Framer Motion for animations. Users click any point on the globe to select coordinates, or choose from 9 real Artemis candidate site presets.

Dual-mode interface:
Explorer Mode features a dark space-themed UI with animated visualizations — a surface viewport showing a lander with animated solar power rays and Earth DTE(direct-to-earth) communication links, a color-coded status strip (gold = power + comms, yellow = power only, blue = comms only, gray = blackout), and educational physics notes.

Planner Mode provides a light-themed, data-dense view with side-by-side configuration comparison, summary statistics tables, and overlaid charts suitable for engineering analysis.

Tools and technologies:
Backend: Python, Flask, NumPy, Requests. Frontend: React, Vite, Three.js/React Three Fiber, Recharts, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion, Axios.

Deployment: Render (backend), Vercel (frontend).

Version control: Git/GitHub. AI tools (Claude, Gemini -- antigravity(agentic coding window), Claude Code for debugging) were used to accelerate code development and instant and comfortable and faster debugging..

Required Links :

1. Github : https://github.com/roboshubhayan200/lunar-selenix

2. Backend API : https://lunar-selenix.onrender.com/

3. Site URL : https://lunar-selenix.vercel.app/

Impact:
This tool democratizes access to lunar site analysis. Mission planners at agencies like NASA, ISRO, or ESA can use it for preliminary site screening. Students and educators can explore how solar geometry and orbital mechanics affect lunar surface operations — concepts that are normally locked behind expensive proprietary software.

Creativity:
Rather than using pre-computed static datasets, Lunar Selenix queries JPL Horizons in real time, meaning it works for any coordinate, any date range, and any step resolution. The dual-mode concept — a single backend powering both an engaging educational interface and a serious engineering tool — is designed to serve the full spectrum of different users as the challenge in the problem statement describes.
